title: "But I'm not a leader"
author: Melissa Muth Martinez
summary: Muth Martinez, founder of Honest Office, argues that many people we most want in leadership opt out because of mistaken messages about what leadership is, who it is for and what it demands. She starts from the view that leadership is a relational act and that organizations hand out titles without tools or support. She lists ten common opt-out statements, such as I hate politics and I am not the loudest person in the room, and translates each into the value or worry beneath it. The thread is that quiet, reflective and relational people have rarely seen a version of leadership that looks right to them. She ends with self-audit questions for aspiring and tenured leaders and with the claim that no one can call themselves a leader until they have helped someone else become one.
points: Leadership is framed as being responsible to people, with accountability, relationships and trust ahead of deliverables.
The ten opt-out phrases are decoded as values (listening, transparency, learning) that leaders have wrongly signaled are not wanted.
Organizations invest little in preparing first-time leaders, handing over a title without tools, support or clarity.
Asking about the impact someone wants to have is proposed in place of asking whether they want to climb the ladder.
The self-audit questions turn the diagnosis into practice for both new and tenured leaders.
quotes: Leadership is a relational act. It’s the thing that happens in the way we guide, support, and nurture the people around us.
Too often, we hand folks a title, but no tools. No support. No clarity on what it means to now be responsible to the people they lead.

I say responsible to versus responsible for intentionally. Leadership needs to be centered around accountability, relationships, and trust, first—before any of the other stuff, like deliverables and outcomes.

Because truthfully, many of the people we actually want and need in formal leadership roles are opting out. It’s not because they lack potential—on the contrary, their potential is significant—but because we’ve sent them the wrong messages about what leadership is, what it requires, and who it’s for.
Translation: I’ve internalized the idea that leadership is a destination we arrive at, rather than a never-ending journey.
What if we told people, early and often, that good leadership starts with a deep sense of care and reflection instead of charisma and readiness?
Leaders have a responsibility to cultivate the next generation. And we shouldn’t forget that we can’t actually call ourselves leaders until we’ve helped someone else get there.
